James Hardie is the industry leader in exterior home and outdoor living solutions, with a portfolio that includes fiber cement, fiber gypsum, composite and PVC decking and railing products. Our family of trusted brands includes Hardie®, TimberTech®, AZEK Exteriors®, Versatex®, fermacell®, and StruXure®. With over 8,000 employees, James Hardie boasts 31 operating sites, 6 recycling facilities, and 6 research and development centers globally. Powered by a dynamic workforce, we're united by our purpose of Building a Better Future for All™ through sustainable innovation, a Zero Harm culture, and a commitment to empowering our people and communities. body_text: View All News The First Bancorp Announces Second Quarter Results July 22, 2026 Net Interest Margin Expansion and Improved Efficiency Lead to an 18.6% Increase in Second Quarter Earnings DAMARISCOTTA, Maine--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- The First Bancorp (Nasdaq: FNLC), ("the Company", "we", "us", "our"), parent company of First National Bank, today reported unaudited results for the quarter and six months ended June 30, 2026. Net income for the second quarter was $9.6 million with fully diluted earnings per share of $0.85, increases of 18.6% and 17.8%, respectively, from net income of $8.1 million and diluted earnings per share of $0.72 for the quarter ended June 30, 2025. Strong earnings for the period were driven by sustained net interest margin expansion, enhanced non-interest income, and disciplined expense control. Year-to-date in 2026, net income was $18.6 million with fully diluted earnings per share of $1.65, increases of 22.5% and 21.7%, respectively, from net income of $15.1 million and earnings per share of $1.35 for the six months ended June 30, 2025. Second Quarter Notable Items: Net Income of $9.6 million is an increase of 18.6% as compared to Q2 2025 Diluted EPS of $0.85 is an increase of 17.8% from Q2 2025 Net Interest Margin expanded to 2.88%, a 36-basis point increase from Q2 2025 Loan growth in the period of $18.6 million Efficiency Ratio of 50.33%, improved from 52.39% in Q2 2025 Tangible Book Value per share rose to $23.25, up 11.0% from Q2 2025 Quarterly shareholder dividend increased to $0.38 per share CEO COMMENTS "I am pleased to report strong year-over-year earnings growth for the second quarter," commented Tony C. McKim, the Company's President and Chief Executive Officer. "Net income of $9.6 million for the second quarter of 2026 represents an increase of 18.6% from the second quarter of 2025. Our Return on Average Assets for the period was 1.20% and our Return on Average Tangible Common Equity was 14.67%, both up nicely from 1.01% and 13.95%, respectively, a year ago." "Our net interest margin improved for the eighth consecutive quarter, to 2.88% for the second quarter of 2026, up 2 basis points in the period and up 36 basis points from the second quarter of 2025. Margin improvement has been focused in stable earning asset yields and reduced funding costs, propelling net interest income up 15.0% from the prior year quarter. Growth in non-interest income, notably wealth management and debit card revenue, was an additional catalyst for the bottom line. Overall revenue growth also drove an improvement in our efficiency ratio to 50.33% for the period as compared to 52.39% a year ago." "Total assets increased $15 million in the quarter, including net loan growth of $19 million. New loan production for the quarter was $131 million, up modestly from the first quarter, as we focus upon pricing discipline and prudent underwriting of new credits. Total deposits increased $15 million in the period, with growth in short-term time deposits being partially offset by a decrease in non-maturity deposits. Non-maturity deposit outflow in the quarter was in line with seasonal patterns. We expect strong local deposit inflow through year-end based on these same patterns, allowing for reduction of higher-cost, short-term funding, helping to sustain margin expansion against recent rate pressure in the market. The Company's capital position is strong, and overall liquidity remains more than sufficient." Concluding, Mr. McKim shared, "We are pleased with the strong operating results produced in the second quarter. As the credit environment and related credit costs normalize off of the extraordinary lows of the past few years, the Bank is well positioned and poised for continued growth." OPERATING RESULTS Q2 2026 v. Q2 2025 (prior year quarter) Net income was $9.6 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, an increase of $1.5 million or 18.6% from the second quarter of 2025. Net interest income was $21.2 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, an increase of $2.8 million or 15.0% from the second quarter of 2025. Net interest margin improved to 2.88% for the second quarter of 2026, up from 2.52% in the prior year quarter. The lift in margin was the result of stable yields on earning assets coupled with a 40-basis point decrease in the cost of total liabilities. Earning assets averaged a yield of 5.34% for the three months ended June 30, 2026, while total liabilities carried an average cost of 2.88%. Total non-interest income was $4.7 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, an increase of $532,000, or 12.9% from the second quarter of 2025. The increase was centered in Wealth Management revenue which was up $212,000 or 15.9% from the prior year on strong growth in assets under management. Debit card revenue increased $89,000 or 6.9%, while other operating income increased $211,000 or 28.2%. Total non-interest expense for the three months ended June 30, 2026, was $13.4 million, an increase of $1.2 million, or 9.7%, from the second quarter of 2025. The period-to-period change is centered in employee salaries and benefits, resulting from annual salary adjustments and higher health insurance expenses. OPERATING RESULTS Q2 2026 v. Q1 2026 (linked quarter) Net income was $9.6 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, an increase of $567,000 or 6.3% from the first quarter of 2026. Net interest income of $21.2 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, was an increase of $473,000 or 2.3% from the linked quarter, resulting from expansion in both average earning assets and net interest margin. Average earning assets grew $10.3 million in the second quarter, while net interest margin increased to 2.88%, an improvement of 2 basis points from the linked quarter. Total non-interest income of $4.7 million for the second quarter of 2026 was up $210,000 from the first quarter of 2026. The increase was centered in Debit Card revenue, which was up $175,000 on strong transaction volume. Revenue increased $62,000 at First National Wealth Management, while other operating income fell $59,000, principally on lower loan-based derivative fees. Total non-interest expense for the three months ended June 30, 2026, was $13.4 million, a decrease of $239,000, or 1.8%, from the first quarter. As compared to the linked quarter, salaries and benefit expense fell $210,000 due to lower payroll taxes and higher deferred salaries, and occupancy expenses fell $120,000 attributable to lower seasonal costs for building maintenance and fuel. LOANS, TOTAL ASSETS & FUNDING Total assets as of June 30, 2026, were $3.22 billion, up $15.3 million in the second quarter. Earning assets grew $9.3 million with loan growth of $18.6 million during the period. Investment balances grew by $17.6 million in the quarter, while overnight funds sold decreased by $27.4 million. Loan balances grew at an annualized rate of 3.10% in the second quarter. The residential mortgage and home equity loan segments each contributed to loan portfolio growth, up $12.0 million and $13.2 million, respectively, during the period. Commercial and industrial loan balances increased $1.0 million, while commercial real estate loan balances and multifamily loan balances decreased by $9.4 million and $10.6 million, respectively. Total deposits as of June 30, 2026, were $2.68 billion, an increase of $15.1 million in the quarter. Non-maturity deposits fell $28.7 million in the second quarter, consistent with seasonal patterns, while time deposits, principally short-term, increased $43.9 million. Borrowed funds increased $18.3 million during the period, mostly in short-term FHLB advances. Uninsured deposits as of June 30, 2026, were estimated at 17.2% of total deposits, and 74% of uninsured deposits were fully collateralized. Available day-one liquidity was $706 million, sufficient to cover 153% of estimated uninsured deposits. ASSET QUALITY Overall asset quality remains satisfactory and was stable in the second quarter. As of June 30, 2026, the ratio of non-performing assets to total assets was 0.54%, up slightly from 0.51% as of March 31, 2026, and compared to 0.19% as of June 30, 2025. The ratio of non-performing loans to total loans was 0.71% as of June 30, 2026, up slightly from 0.67% as of March 31, 2026, and compared to 0.25% as of June 30, 2025. Loans past due thirty days or more improved to 0.93% of total loans as of June 30, 2026, down from 1.14% as of March 31, 2026. The Allowance for Credit Losses ("ACL") on loans stood at 1.01% of total loans as of June 30, 2026, down slightly from the linked quarter and prior year quarter. A provision for credit losses of $919,000 was recorded in the second quarter of 2026. Net loan charge-offs in the second quarter totaled $1.6 million concentrated within a single credit relationship. Year-to-date, net charge-offs represent an annualized 0.20% of total loans. CAPITAL The Company’s regulatory capital position was strong as of June 30, 2026. The Leverage Capital ratio increased to an estimated 9.21% as of June 30, 2026, as compared to the 9.09% and 8.48% reported as of March 31, 2026, and as of June 30, 2025, respectively. The estimated Total Risk-Based Capital ratio was 14.24% as of June 30, 2026, as compared to the 14.05% and 13.31% reported as of March 31, 2026, and as of June 30, 2025, respectively. The Company's tangible book value per share was $23.25 as of June 30, 2026, up from $22.71 as of March 31, 2026, and up from $20.94 as of June 30, 2025. The Tangible Common Equity ratio increased to 8.23% as of June 30, 2026, up from 8.08% as of March 31, 2026, and 7.41% as of June 30, 2025. DIVIDEND On June 25, 2026, the Company's Board of Directors declared a second quarter dividend of $0.38 per share. The dividend was paid on July 17, 2026, to shareholders of record as of July 7, 2026. ABOUT THE FIRST BANCORP The First Bancorp, the parent company of First National Bank, is based in Damariscotta, Maine. Founded in 1864, First National Bank is a full-service community bank with $3.19 billion in assets. The Bank provides a complete array of commercial and retail banking services through eighteen locations in mid-coast and eastern Maine. First National Wealth Management, a division of the Bank, provides investment management and trust services to individuals, businesses, and municipalities. More information about The First Bancorp, First National Bank and First National Wealth Management may be found at www.thefirst.com . Financial Measures Certain information in this release contains financial information determined by methods other than in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (“GAAP”). Management uses these “non-GAAP” measures in its analysis of the Company's performance (including for purposes of determining the compensation of certain executive officers and other Company employees) and believes that these non-GAAP financial measures provide a greater understanding of ongoing operations and enhance comparability of results with prior periods and with other financial institutions, as well as demonstrating the effects of significant gains and charges in the current period, in light of the disclosure practices employed by many other publicly-traded financial institutions. The Company believes that a meaningful analysis of its financial performance requires an understanding of the factors underlying that performance. Management believes that investors may use these non-GAAP financial measures to analyze financial performance without the impact of unusual items that may obscure trends in the Company's underlying performance. These disclosures should not be viewed as a substitute for operating results determined in accordance with GAAP, nor are they necessarily comparable to non-GAAP performance measures that may be presented by other companies. In several places net interest income is calculated on a fully tax-equivalent basis. Specifically included in interest income was tax-exempt interest income from certain investment securities and loans. An amount equal to the tax benefit derived from this tax-exempt income has been added back to the interest income total which, as adjusted, increased net interest income accordingly. Management believes the disclosure of tax-equivalent net interest income information improves the clarity of financial analysis, and is particularly useful to investors in understanding and evaluating the changes and trends in the Company's results of operations. Other financial institutions commonly present net interest income on a tax-equivalent basis. This adjustment is considered helpful in the comparison of one financial institution's net interest income to that of another institution, as each will have a different proportion of tax-exempt interest from its earning assets. Moreover, net interest income is a component of a second financial measure commonly used by financial institutions, net interest margin, which is the ratio of net interest income to average earning assets. For purposes of this measure as well, other financial institutions generally use tax-equivalent net interest income to provide a better basis of comparison from institution to institution. The Company follows these practices. title: CMMC Level 2: Do you really need FedRAMP for your IAM?
summary: Is commercial IAM sufficient for CMMC Level 2? Learn how C3PAOs evaluate Security Protection Assets (SPAs) and FIPS 140-2 requirements.
body_text: Topics FedRAMP Table of Contents Share Ready to make Identity a business advantage? Sign up today. Get started TL;DR: Relying on commercial identity and access management (IAM) platforms for CMMC Level 2 compliance introduces significant audit risks. Although some auditors classify non-FedRAMP identity tools as security protection assets (SPAs), strict Certified Third-party Assessment Organization (C3PAO) often treat identity providers as external service providers (ESPs). To ensure audit success, those building their CMMC Level 2 architecture should deploy FedRAMP Moderate or High authorized identity environments that provide official Bodies of Evidence (BoE) and FIPS 140-2 validated cryptography. I’ve been working with customers for a while now, and I’ve noticed a trend: some consultants believe that Okta (within the context of CMMC L2) doesn’t need to hit FedRAMP Moderate standards. In my (not so) humble opinion—that’s concerning. Your IAM system represents the “keys to the kingdom”—it's not something you want to leave unprotected. While those consultants are technically correct on a strict reading of the regulation, relying on that limiting assertion introduces significant risk when it comes to the audit. The debate centers on a very specific nuance in the CMMC Scoping Guide regarding how different cloud applications are categorized. The consultant’s argument: Security protection assets vs. cloud service providers Auditors who make this argument are zeroing in on a specific technicality: the difference between a cloud service provider (CSP) that stores your actual data and a security protection asset (SPA) that just manages access. The DFARS 7012 trigger: As written, the Defense Federal Acquisition Supplement (DFARS) 252.204-7012(b)(2)(ii)(D) only mandates FedRAMP Moderate for external cloud providers used to "store, process, or transmit" Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). Okta’s role: An IAM platform like Okta processes usernames, passwords, and multi-factor authentication (MFA) tokens—it does not store or transmit your actual CUI (like military schematics or contract details). The Scoping Guide ruling: In the official CMMC Level 2 Scoping Guide, tools that provide security capabilities but don't hold CUI are categorized as SPAs. The guide explicitly states that SPAs must be assessed against relevant NIST SP 800-171 controls, but it does not explicitly stamp them with the strict DFARS 7012 FedRAMP Moderate requirement. Because of this regulatory nuance, some consultants argue that as long as you can prove Okta is configured securely and satisfies the Identification & Authentication (IA) controls of NIST SP 800-171, the underlying Okta cloud doesn't need a FedRAMP stamp of approval. Why relying on this loophole is risky It might hold up on paper, but betting your CMMC assessment on a non-FedRAMP-certified IAM is a high-stakes gamble. Here is why: The "keys to the kingdom" reality Okta governs access to the systems that do hold CUI (such as your GovCloud environment or local servers). If an attacker breaches your IAM layer, they gain direct access to your CUI. Many strict C3PAOs view any cloud service capable of granting access to CUI as an external service provider (ESP), inherently pulling it back into the FedRAMP Moderate bucket. The cryptographic requirements (FIPS 140-2) To pass CMMC Level 2, any cryptography used to protect data—including the transmission and protection of authentication credentials—must be encrypted to the FIPS 140-2 validation standard. Most non-FedRAMP-certified IAMs in the market do not utilize FIPS-validated cryptographic modules by default. To get guaranteed FIPS compliance, you generally have to move to a federally aligned platform. Okta already built a solution for this Okta itself recognizes this hurdle. We built Okta for US Military and Okta Government Cloud , which hold FedRAMP Moderate, FedRAMP High , and DoD Impact Level 5 (IL5) authorizations. Because a fully compliant federal version exists, a defense assessor will question why a contractor protected DoD-related access paths using the commercial tier. Furthermore, our FedRAMP High and IL5 offerings meet the International Traffic in Arms (ITAR) requirements for “US persons.” Okta strictly boundaries its compliance artifacts based on our product tiers: Okta Commercial cloud: We do not maintain a FedRAMP-aligned Body of Evidence (BoE) or 3PAO assessment for our commercial cloud. So, if your auditor requests backend security attestations to prove NIST SP 800-171/172 equivalence, the Okta Commercial cloud will not be able to provide them. Okta for Government (Moderate/High) and Okta for US Military: These are isolated, dedicated environments. We actively maintain and provide the official FedRAMP packages and agency Authorizations to Operate (ATOs) for these tiers. Federal and defense entities can request these packages directly through tools such as connect.gov or eMASS to hand over to their auditors. The bottom line If you’re currently building out your CMMC Level 2 architecture, my advice is simple: don't cut corners on your IAM provider . While you might find a permissive auditor willing to accept the Okta Commercial cloud as an SPA without a FedRAMP certificate, the safer, future-proof play is to utilize Okta’s FedRAMP Moderate/High-authorized identity solution. If you use anything that isn’t FedRAMP certified, you’re going to have to thoroughly document its isolation, create a bulletproof System Security Plan (SSP) narrative, and ensure your crypto implementations utilize FIPS-validated cryptography. Choose a secure path to federal compliance Securing access paths for critical federal and military operations shouldn’t be a compromise. Implementing our dedicated, compliant identity solutions ensures your organization meets the most stringent federal requirements and is protected against sophisticated identity threats. We deliver the exact level of assurance your auditors expect, without sacrificing the user-friendly experience of modern IAM systems. Download the Okta for Government High datasheet to learn how to adhere to the highest FedRAMP standards and rapidly deploy modern MFA. Download the Okta for US Military datasheet to discover how to centralize secure access to CUI and protect against tactical edge deployments. About the Author Naveed Mirza Senior Solutions Architect Naveed is a Senior Solutions Architect focusing on the DoD and Federal customer base. He has worked in cybersecurity since leaving the US Navy in the late 1990s. Before coming to Okta, Naveed was a consultant for several DoD customers, and he continues to offer advice via active participation in the DoD community. He grew up in Stafford, Virginia, and upon returning from active duty, took up residence there once more. In his free time, he enjoys beer brewing, gaming, and the occasional date night with his wife.

title: Off the Rack: Affordable Classics Designed by Three Italian Icons
summary: Everyone loves a bargain, especially when it comes with a designer label. The entire fashion industry is predicated on the concept of top designers who create haute couture collections in limited quantities at stratospheric prices for the most discerning clients (read: the richest), creating a brand aura that allows them to sell higher-volume ready-to-wear—also known […]
body_text: Everyone loves a bargain, especially when it comes with a designer label. The entire fashion industry is predicated on the concept of top designers who create haute couture collections in limited quantities at stratospheric prices for the most discerning clients (read: the richest), creating a brand aura that allows them to sell higher-volume ready-to-wear—also known as off-the-rack—apparel and accessories for the general public. Once upon a time, the auto industry operated in much the same way. Masterpieces of design (and engineering and performance) such as the Lamborghini Miura and the Ferrari Daytona were the province of the rich, while the rest of us enjoyed them only in pictures in magazines, as we might have admired Elizabeth Taylor in a Givenchy gown in a tabloid photo. And although neither Lamborghini nor Ferrari offered affordable cars for the masses, the men who designed their unattainable cars liberally peddled their skills to mainstream automotive manufacturers across the globe. To continue the fashion analogy, these arrangements were akin to fashion designers today making guest appearances at Uniqlo, the chic yet highly affordable retailer. These occasional collections feature the perspective and talent of the best stylists at fast-fashion prices. Valentino tastes on Uniqlo budgets are nothing new to car enthusiasts, as evidenced by the automobiles we’ve gathered here. Hailing from three manufacturers on three continents, all were conceived by some of the most storied designers—or progettisti , in Italy. Each of these cars bears the design language of legends, but, just like when they were new, they don’t require a second mortgage on your house to put into your garage. 1971–89 Fiat X1/9: A Fiat for Every Man Blair Bunting Designed by Bertone Nuccio Bertone saw great success with the Fiat 850 Coupe and Spider in 1965. When he returned to Fiat’s co-director of design, Oscar Montabone, in the late 1960s with a proposal to make a mid-engine sports car, Montabone wanted none of it. “All you want to do is build a poor man’s Miura,” he said with a sniff, according to Luciano Greggio’s book, Bertone . Nuccio’s dream of forging a relationship with Ferruccio Lamborghini similar to that between Pininfarina and Ferrari had flamed out with Ferruccio’s waning interest in the car business. It looked as though his attempt with Fiat was destined to do the same. Fiat issued marching orders for only two new design concepts on the existing 128 chassis, one front-engine and one rear-. Nuccio was told he could produce a mid-engine design if he wanted to, but not to hold his breath about it being made. Fiat was historically a front- or rear-engine company—the 850 and its 500, 750, and 800 predecessors were all rear-engine cars. With Marcello Gandini, then chief designer at Bertone, at the helm, the mid-engine undertaking was in capable hands. Gandini had already designed the Miura for Lamborghini and went on to create numerous mid-engine cars, including the Alfa Romeo Carabo concept and the Countach. Nuccio’s persistence and Gandini’s designs wore Montabone down, but Nuccio didn’t get everything he wanted by the time the X1/9 went on sale in the U.S. in 1973. He’d hoped to make the car bigger than the Spider to appeal to American buyers. Nuccio expressed concerns that it would be too small and considered more of a toy that landed “in the hands of students and secretaries.” The Fiat X1/9’s instrument panel is a pure period piece. Blair Bunting Its richly colored leather seats with fabric inserts have timeless appeal. Blair Bunting “The X1/9 was my first new car. I bought it in college in 1980,” said Rick Polhamus, one such student and owner of the brown X1/9 you see here. “It was black-on-black, and it was great. I never had to drive anyone to parties because there was no room.” His dad told him that this was the only time in his life that he wasn’t going to need four seats, so he might as well buy something with two. Polhamus only sold that original car because he moved to sweltering Palm Springs, California, for a job and needed A/C. A few years ago, when friends started buying project cars, Polhamus got the itch to own an X1/9 again. His new car, a 1980 model, arrived on a truck after he bought it from an online auction site for $5200. “As it was coming down the ramp,” he recalled, “I thought they’d made a mistake because it was so much smaller than I’d remembered.” Nuccio’s size-matters concerns were clearly well-founded. Gandini had joined Bertone at 26, apprenticing under fellow design legend Giorgetto Giugiaro for a year before Giugiaro left to open his own studio (we’ll get to him shortly). One glance at Gandini’s Autobianchi A112 Runabout concept car and the DNA connection to the X1/9 appears clear. It struck the same clean-cut silhouette but wasn’t as sharp a wedge as, say, the Lancia Stratos. It sported the same beak as the Runabout, with a long overhang and pop-up headlights instead of the bizarro headlight pods placed on the concept’s C-pillars. The X1/9 wore an integrated spoiler up front and had a targa hardtop that was stowed in a special compartment at the front of the car. The Runabout’s tiny windscreen was replaced with traditional A-pillars and a proper windshield. Sharp exterior lines define a surprisingly comfortable cabin. Blair Bunting This new car retained its factory code name, X1/9, derived from Fiat’s convoluted project numbering system intended to keep auto journalists off the scent of new products. When Montabone finally presented it to Fiat owner Gianni Agnelli, he loved it. “Don’t touch anything,” Agnelli reportedly said. “I like it very much the way it is.” “The name Bertone didn’t mean anything to me necessarily,” Polhamus admitted about his X1/9’s origins. “Later, I understood what that meant. It just validated my feelings about it. In 1980, nothing looked like it.” To him, it was revolutionary. “The angular wedge with its sharp edges made it stand out,” said Polhamus, who was studying architecture when he bought it. The sticker price of the 1980 X1/9 was about $8190, or some $34,000 today. By 1980, the engine grew to a 1.5-liter four-cylinder that made 75 horsepower after Fiat ditched the Weber carburetor for fuel injection. It’s a smooth driver, with well-apportioned gear ratios and short throws. It revs high even with a five-speed and is so low to the ground, it makes you feel like a cat zooming down San Francisco hills on a skateboard. Flickr/Alden Jewell “The X1/9 drives like a Formula 1 car,” said F1 world champion Emerson Fittipaldi when he first reviewed it for Italian magazine Quattroruote . “Only rarely have I come across this kind of honest roadholding.” He cooed about its weight distribution and neutral handling but did criticize its lack of torque. Although the X1/9 is petite, it’s surprisingly practical, with enough trunk space in the front and rear to accommodate a weekender bag or two. A trunk lock in the driver’s door jamb, which utilizes a secondary key, keeps your belongings secure. And it looks so good, you might never put the roof on. “Even in the winter, the thermal cover [the cocoon effect of the compact cabin] is so efficient, as the warm air from the heater gets trapped, you could be driving around in a T-shirt,” Polhamus said. Despite Polhamus having regrets about selling his original car, buying a replacement in modern times did not break his bank. Hagerty data pegs a 1980 X1/9 at about $10,700 for a #3 example. 1987–93 Cadillac Allanté: Detroit Returns to Turin Blair Bunting Designed by Pininfarina Few automotive origin stories are as outlandish, nonsensical, and expensive as the Cadillac Allanté’s. Looking for a sleek two-door to compete with the Mercedes-Benz SL and Jaguar XJS, Robert Burger, then Cadillac’s general manager, looked to Italian coachbuilder Pininfarina for help. Burger wanted something open-aired and European-looking to sit atop the Eldorado architecture. Battista “Pinin” Farina—“pinin” in northern Italian slang means youngest—started his company in 1930 after separating from his brother’s Stabilimenti Industriali Farina coachworks. Upon opening the doors, Pininfarina built bodies for Rolls-Royce, Lancia (whose founder, Vincenzo Lancia, helped Battista start his company), Hispano-Suiza, and Fiat, among others. It was the 1947 Cisitalia 202 Coupé, with its low hood sweeping back from an elegant nose, that put the coachbuilder on auto manufacturers’ wish lists. In the early 1950s, the relationship between Pininfarina and Ferrari began producing cars, culminating in milestones such as the 250 GT SWB, the Daytona, the Testarossa, and the F40. The Allanté’s clunky steering wheel, set against a backdrop of one of GM’s 1980s asymmetrical instrument pods, must have seemed like a good idea at the time. It does at least provide good sightlines to the tachometer and speedometer. Oh, that gearshift lever. Blair Bunting It was this mystique that GM executives sought to highlight a new era of design and technology for Cadillac. And the partnership had some history—Pininfarina and Cadillac had already worked together on the Eldorado Brougham in 1959. Thirty years later, the renewed collaboration resulted in the Allanté and what Cadillac manufacturing operations director Bill Buschman called “the longest assembly line in the world.” Step one: The chassis and wiring harnesses were flown from Detroit to a newly built factory just outside Turin, the northern Italian epicenter of automotive manufacturing. Step two: The Italians constructed the Allanté’s body panels, married them to the chassis, and then painted them. Step three: Cars were then transported to San Giorgio, about an hour-and-a-half drive from Turin, where they were wired up and trimmed with carpet and upholstery. Step four: The finished bodies were trucked back to Turin, where they boarded one of two specially designed Alitalia and Lufthansa 747s , which flew them to Michigan, where the Detroit-Hamtramck Assembly Center installed their powertrains. At first, the planes could accommodate 56 cars. After a retrofit, they squeezed in 59. Step five: Finished cars drove a 1-mile test track before they rolled onto a fleet of carriers to dealers. By the time it reached a dealership, an Allanté already had more than 7000 miles on it, mostly in the air. The transatlantic production process that produced the Cadillac roadster is one of the most fascinating examples of Italian-American automotive collaboration. GM When Tom Rohner, owner of the 1993 Allanté we drove and photographed, first heard this story, like many, he was intrigued. “They’d put four or five Allantés together on the line at the [Pininfarina] factory, then spit out a Testarossa,” Rohner said. “Both models went through the same paint shop.” In 1987, Rohner drove his father’s brand-new Allanté and was hooked. Within a year, he’d bought a 1988 model. A couple of years later, after a move to San Diego, he and his dad bought a parts car, as repairs were already proving expensive. Once everyone in the national club found out about it, his phone started ringing off the hook. Before long, Rohner owned six parts cars and started a club. Now he self-publishes a magazine called Roadsters by Cadillac . “I’ve dismantled 66 Allantés myself,” Rohner said. So extensive is his knowledge, he can tell instantly if someone with the wrong mechanical background has worked on a particular car. Blair Bunting Blair Bunting Exterior lines from Pininfarina’s Italian design masters have aged far better than the instrument panel. Blair Bunting The Allanté was the most expensive American car, with a base price of about $50,000 in 1987, some $145,000 in today’s dollars. It had to feel special, so Cadillac threw everything at it. The 1987 model had an advanced version of Bosch’s anti-lock braking system. A three-mode automatically adjusted suspension came in 1988. The 1990 Allanté had the brand’s first CD player and was the first front-wheel-drive car with traction control. Cadillac used the Allanté to test features before putting them in higher-volume cars. The sumptuous, bolstered leather seats are luxurious to the touch. The December 1986 issue of the British magazine What Car? suggested the Allanté was “built for two six-foot Texans… the Recaro seats are designed for their posteriors, so they’re big rather than hip hugging.” The fully carpeted trunk holds golf bags aplenty—this alone should have been American catnip. Given the number of buttons on the dash, you might expect the Allanté to take off back to Turin on autopilot. From the leather-covered shifter with its hand-stitching to the curved dash nook on the passenger side, the Allanté worked the details right. Flickr/IFHP97 Flickr/IFHP97 Mario Vernacchia, Pininfarina design manager for the Allanté, executed an exterior that defined the simple elegance of the period—even Vernacchia’s Ferrari Mondial was considered an example of excessive restraint. Sadly, for all its innovations and design pedigree, the Allanté wasn’t a hot ticket. The lofty sales goal of 6000 units a year was never met. In 1987, in addition to Rohner’s dad, only around 3000 others bought one. It wasn’t until the final year of production, 1993, when Cadillac installed the more powerful Northstar V-8, that sales peaked at slightly under 4700 units. The Northstar allowed the Allanté finally to deliver on Burger’s sporty European premise. Sprawling majestically under the hood with its four cams and 32 valves, it made 290 horsepower, an upgrade from the 200 horses of the Allanté’s 4.5-liter, which had already replaced the original pushrod 4.1-liter V-8 and its 170 horses in 1988. After the Northstar went in, only the Viper and the Corvette had more giddy-up among American roadsters at the time. Marketplace/BlakeWingrove Twist the key and the V-8’s exhaust burble sounds exactly as the exterior looks, enough to turn a head but perhaps not snap a neck. The Northstar engine answers the throttle pedal’s call well, even if the suspension leans to the cushiony end of the touring spectrum during a 7.2-second voyage to 60 mph. The Northstar V-8 is notorious for costly head-gasket failures, but Rohner demurred. Of the almost 100 Cadillacs with Northstar engines he’s owned, he’s never had a head-gasket problem. In all his years working on them, only two customers needed to have the head gasket redone. “They made improvements to the car every year,” Rohner said. “And when they got it just about right, they quit making it.” General Motors excels at this enterprise, deleting cars including the Buick Grand National, the Pontiac Fiero, and the Chevrolet Impala SS right when they were getting good. They’re at it again with the Cadillac Blackwing engine heading into retirement before the end of this year. Rohner credits the Allanté’s semiautomatic convertible top design for some of the car’s sales woes. “It requires more manual labor than stump removal,” he said. He demonstrated the cumbersome 1-plus-minute choreography to retract the roof by awkwardly pulling things up and pushing other things down, all while leaning over the car. You won’t hear him complain too much, though. “I rebuild at least two of these rear pull-down units a week,” he said, pointing to the motorized contraption that secures the top in place when reemployed. “I send the designer a Christmas card every year.” In today’s market, Hagerty values an Allanté at approximately $16,200 (in #2 excellent condition). So yes, the Allanté is now an Italian-designer steal. 1992–97 Subaru SVX: All-Wheel Magnifico Blair Bunting Designed by Giugiaro After cutting his teeth in the late ’60s on the softer, curvier shapes of the Iso Grifo and the Maserati Ghibli, Giorgetto Giugiaro started pinching and triangulating cars for the wedge era. The noses of his Maserati Boomerang and Alfa Romeo Iguana concepts looked as if they could scrape ice off a windshield. After stints at Bertone and Ghia, Giugiaro branched out on his own in 1968, founding Italdesign Giugiaro. Though known for his pricier collector car designs and noteworthy concepts, Giugiaro’s later work regularly appeared in the showrooms of whoever would pay to keep the lights on. We can thank him for the Volkswagen Golf Mk I and Scirocco, the Fiat Panda, the first-generation Impulse from Isuzu, and even the original Lexus GS. Subaru teamed Giugiaro with staff designers Tetsuya Hayashi and Hiroshi Sarukawa to transform the polarizing mid-’80s XT sports coupe. The result: the flagship SVX coupe, which was designed in Italy and engineered in Japan, with the concept debuting at the 1989 Tokyo Motor Show. The production model was introduced in the U.S. in the summer of 1991 as a ’92 model. The SVX’s cabin, with its double-decker stereo hiding discreetly behind a wood door, has aged well. Blair Bunting In 2001, David Barnblatt saw this red 1997 SVX on eBay Motors, advertised as the last new production example, with only 200 miles and an asking price of $50,000. A decade later, the same car showed up again at a Subaru dealer in Oakland, California, with only 36,000 miles on the odometer and a far more reasonable $7700 price. It reminded Barnblatt of the late ’80s JDM (Japanese Domestic Market) forbidden fruit he’d read about in car magazines, except now it was produce he could finally afford. “I was blown away by the SVX’s quality and design,” Barnblatt recalled. “It was not like a normal Subaru. This was built to a different standard, more like a Mercedes. The way the doors closed, the interior, everything felt special.” Interior suede-like trim was a rare touch in the 1990s. Blair Bunting The SVX sports squinting headlights, a heavier back end, and a massive greenhouse. A lower body line creates a crease in the front fender that transitions to the windowsill then continues to the top of the rear decklid—all in the name of accentuating the wedge. The car came with two distinct pairs of wheels, the blades of each being specific to the right and left sides of the car, an element both practical for cooling purposes and pleasing to the eye. The optional integrated rear wing looks sculptural in nature. The most striking feature of the SVX might be the unconventional “glass-to-glass” canopy, a design similarly found in Giugiaro’s 1983 Renault Gabbiano concept. The lower part of the window retracts into the doors, yet the upper glass remains fixed onto the doorframe. This allowed for excellent visibility while maximizing aerodynamics and giving it a singular look. The side windowsills sit noticeably lower behind the delicate A-pillars, giving off jet-fighter cockpit vibes. Early models had a black roof, which added to the effect. “Subaru has not built a homogenized blahmobile,” Road & Track gushed in a 1992 review. The cabin was designed to wrap around the driver—another aircraft attribute. “With the half-window open, when it’s raining, no water gets in the car,” Barnblatt said. You’re protected by the front piece of stationary glass. Even the engine bay looks aesthetically pleasing, not overrun by wires and hoses. You’re met with Subaru’s big, torquey EG33 engine, a 230-hp, 3.3-liter horizontally opposed flat-six, which made power akin to the contemporary midrange trims of competitors such as the Dodge Stealth and the Nissan 300ZX. The 3.3-liter horizontally opposed flat-six engine provided grand touring, rather than sports car, vibes. Blair Bunting From the driver’s seat, the SVX delivers on its touring car résumé, with tall gearing and a silken ride, all while the engine hovers at 2000 rpm. It provides great outward visibility, the A/C blows perfectly, and it can go 400 to 500 miles on its 18.5-gallon fuel tank. Its speed-sensitive steering, which adds weight at speed, predates traditional Sport drive modes that achieve a similar effect. All-wheel drive was standard on most models; a cheaper front-drive option was available for a brief period, but few bought it. At a time when most sporty coupes were offered with a manual gearbox, the SVX came only with an automatic. Subaru produced some 25,000 SVXs from 1992 to 1997, of which about 14,000 came to the U.S. Only 600 were made in the final year as production wound down. Originally, the SVX didn’t come cheap, with a sticker price of $37,000—a fair chunk of change in 1992. Adjusted for inflation, that’s $87,000, making the SVX one of the most expensive Subarus ever produced. Hagerty Valuation lists an excellent #2 SVX at about $18,200. Barnblatt concedes there might not be much of a market now for his Japanese/Italian unicorn. “Kids who bought them and thought it would be a fast car or something they could drift are disappointed.” *** Naturally, we’ll always love the supercars in posters we taped to our walls as teenagers, the same way we might daydream of grand Lake Como villas, aged bottles of Brunello di Montalcino, or an Armani suit. But there’s also something transcendent about Italy’s attainable charms—a walk through a piazza at dusk, a scoop of strac-ciatella gelato, or a drive in an affordable designer sports car. These pleasures might be inexpensive, but they’re by no means any less Italian. This story appeared in print in the July/August issue of Hagerty Drivers Club magazine. title: Nike’s New Kobe x FC Barcelona Kit Is Built for a Club That Plays Without Fear
summary: Nike is unveiling the Kobe x FC Barcelona 2026–27 away kit and collection, which bring together the Kobe Sheath and Barça crest for the second consecutive season.
body_text: Nike is bringing together the Kobe Sheath and Barça crest for the second consecutive season, joining Kobe Bryant’s legendary Mamba Mentality with FC Barcelona’s enduring pursuit of excellence in an away kit and collection for a club that plays without fear. The partnership builds on the inaugural Kobe x FC Barcelona collection , which introduced the Kobe Sheath to professional football for the first time, extending a shared dedication to changing the game and inspiring the next generation of athletes. The 2026–27 kit channels Kobe’s Mamba Mentality through details designed to be seen and felt, giving athletes confidence backed by proof. A black mamba texture nods to Kobe’s relentless work ethic, while a Field Purple base carries forward the color he made iconic. Gold accents are rooted in a never-ending quest for championships, and an iridescent crest serves as a reminder of the attention to detail required to win at the highest level. One of Kobe’s most enduring messages is inscribed at the inner collar as a fitting call to athletes who don’t see fear as an option and understand glory is earned by putting in the work: “Leave the game better than you found it.” Further, the kit is built with Nike’s Aero-FIT performance cooling technology , which leverages lightweight breathability to help athletes perform at their peak, no matter the conditions . A full suite of training apparel and sportswear bring the partners’ dedication to excellence from the pitch to the street and beyond, including jackets, T-shirts, a hoodie, jogger, short and wide-leg pant, all sporting the Kobe Sheath and Barça crest. Similar motifs also anchor exclusive FC Barcelona expressions of two classic Nike footwear silhouettes, the Dunk Low and Kobe 3. Entering its second season, the collaboration celebrates Kobe’s lifelong love for football and admiration for FC Barcelona’s joyful style of play and philosophy. In return, Barça continues to recognize Kobe as a driving force in global sport who lived by the discipline and drive for greatness that defines the club. The new Kobe x FC Barcelona kit will be available globally July 24 at nike.com , Barça Official Stores and select Nike retail locations.

title: SEI Expands ETF Platform with SEI QiM U.S. Equity Factor Allocation Active ETF (SEUS)
summary: Established Dynamic Active Multifactor Strategy Extends QiM's Time-Tested Investment Process Through Single-Ticker ETF Solution OAKS, Pa., July…...
body_text: Established Dynamic Active Multifactor Strategy Extends QiM's Time-Tested Investment Process Through Single-Ticker ETF Solution OAKS, Pa. , July 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SEI ® (NASDAQ:SEIC) today announced the launch of the SEI QiM U.S. Equity Factor Allocation Active ETF (NASDAQ:SEUS), an actively managed core U.S. equity solution that brings SEI's established U.S. Equity Factor Allocation strategy to the ETF market. Managed by SEI's Quantitative Investment Management (QiM) team, SEUS provides access to a time-tested investment process through a transparent, cost-effective ETF structure that offers accessibility, scalability, and tax efficiency. SEUS is based on the same dynamic active factor allocation approach that QiM has implemented across other investment vehicles, combining dynamic factor allocation, active stock selection, and disciplined risk management within a diversified equity portfolio. Designed as a core equity allocation, the ETF seeks to adapt as market conditions evolve while maintaining exposure to historically rewarded factors through a risk-aware investment process. Powered by SEI's Quantitative Investment Management team, which manages more than $30 billion in quantitative investment strategies as of March 31, 2026, SEUS leverages proprietary factor research, integrated risk models, and dedicated portfolio management oversight. The launch extends an established investment process through a flexible, transparent, and tax-efficient ETF structure, providing investors with access to the same underlying philosophy, research framework, and portfolio management expertise. Commenting on the ETF launch, Robert Hum, Head of Investment Product and Commercialization at SEI, said: "Markets are increasingly dynamic, and investors need strategies that can adapt alongside them. SEUS expands access to QiM's established investment process, bringing a time-tested active multifactor strategy to investors through a transparent, tax-efficient, single-ticker ETF solution. By combining dynamic factor allocation, active stock selection, and disciplined risk management, SEUS is designed to help investors navigate evolving market environments while maintaining diversified U.S. equity exposure."
